title: Fortune and misfortune
hook: misfortune is where fortune rests; fortune hides misfortune (Tao Te Ching 58)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the more laws: the more prohibitions, the poorer the people. Your line was fewer rules. Which rule did you let go of? Day one thousand one hundred twenty.

An old man lives near the frontier, and one morning his horse runs off across the border. The neighbors come by to say how sorry they are. He shrugs. Who's to say this isn't good luck? That story comes from a different Chinese book, and it's a fitting way to close this week. A week of the small and the soft: seeing the small, the weeds in the fields, the well planted, the newborn's grip, the quiet knower, the sage who meddles less. Today, chapter fifty-eight takes a soft stance toward luck itself.
screen: `A HORSE RUNS OFF.` → `WHO'S TO SAY?` → `A WEEK OF THE SMALL AND SOFT.`

segments.voice: First, the hinge of the chapter. In the Chinese, misfortune is what fortune leans on, and fortune is where misfortune lies hidden. James Legge renders it as two cries: misery, with happiness right beside it; happiness, with misery lurking underneath. Then he asks: "Who knows what either will come to in the end?" Second, the chapter's reason for asking. There's no fixed rule here, it says. What's correct turns strange, and what's good turns ominous. And it adds, a little wearily, that people have been confused about this for a long time. Third, the rest of the frontier story, from the book called the Huainanzi. The runaway horse comes back, bringing a fine horse with it. The neighbors cheer. The old man asks who's to say this isn't bad luck. His son rides the new horse, falls, and breaks his leg. The neighbors grieve. Who's to say, the old man asks. Then war comes, the young men are taken to fight, and the son, lame, stays home. Every turn of the wheel looks final while it's happening. None of them is. Fourth, how the chapter says to live inside that. The sage, it says, is square without cutting anyone, has edges without wounding, is straight without overreaching, and shines without dazzling. In other words: hold your shape, but don't judge too fast. In daily life, that might mean meeting a rejection letter, a canceled trip or a sudden windfall with the same steady question. Not a cheerful one. Just an honest one: who can tell yet?
screen: `FORTUNE LEANS ON MISFORTUNE.` · `NO FIXED RULE.` · `THE HORSE, THE LEG, THE WAR.` · `SQUARE WITHOUT CUTTING.` · then, large: `WHO KNOWS WHAT EITHER WILL COME TO?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look again at one bad break. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one thing that went wrong, recently or long ago. A job that didn't come through. A move you didn't want. A plan that fell apart. Hold it the way you'd hold an old photograph. Don't force it into a blessing; it may have been plain loss, and that's allowed. Just ask, gently: what grew next to it? What else did it lead to? Then let the question stay open for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Fortune and misfortune. Chapter fifty-eight: misfortune is what fortune leans on, and fortune is where misfortune hides. Who knows what either will come to in the end? Today's word.
Your line: who can tell. When something today looks like good news or bad news, say it once, quietly: who can tell yet? Day one thousand one hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching pair chapter fifty-eight with the frontier-horse story from the Huainanzi, as a teaching to hold judgments of good and bad luck loosely.

The frontier-horse story (塞翁失馬) is attributed to the Huainanzi, chapter 18 (人間訓). Confirm attribution and the retelling (horse returns with a fine horse; son falls and breaks his leg; war comes and he is spared). The story's own count of casualties is deliberately left out.
'People have been confused about this for a long time' paraphrases chapter 58's 人之迷，其日固久; confirm.
